_description:
# Who am I

Finding your own name, what is in your stack, and what you are allowed to change.

You are one proc on one daemon. The daemon's table has one row for you: your name, your phase (running, stopped, sleeping), your workspace, your definition, your stack.

Your name: you do not know it from the inside. The command `aos-agent ctl who` looks at `$AOS_STACK`, finds the table row whose stack contains it, and prints the name. Tools that act on you (such as `self_tools`) do this for you, so you rarely need it yourself.

What is in your stack (`$AOS_STACK`):

- `history.jsonl`: your conversation, one JSON message per line. Append only; never rewrite it.
- `queue/`: your queue. Humans and other agents drop letters here; you answer them in order.
- `tools.json`: your own tool registry. It holds only the differences from the definition's (`"$override"` points at that file; a tool you removed is `null`). Written by tools, not by hand.
- `llm.json`: your brain overlay (for example which model you use).
- `system.txt`: your own system text, when you set one (it replaces the definition's whole).
- `tools/<name>/`: a scratch folder for each tool you call.

What you may change: only your own overlays, and only through tools:

- your toolbox: tool `self_tools`, called like `{"op": "add", "name": "<name>", "path": "tools/<name>"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_tools`.
- your brain settings: tool `self_llm`, called like `{"op": "ls"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_llm`.
- your system text: tool `self_system`, called like `{"op": "get"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_system`.
- your conversation history: tool `self_history`, called like `{"op": "ls"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_history`.
- your hooks (programs run when something happens to you): tool `self_hook`, called like `{"op": "ls"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_hook`.
- whether you go on: tool `self_ctl`, called like `{"op": "stop"}`; all calls and rules are in `aos/me.json#/self_ctl`.

To look at yourself (name, phase, tools, history size, mailbox, children, resources), call `self_state` with `{}`; see `aos/me.json#/self_state`.

What you may not change: the definition folder, other agents' stacks, the daemon's files, `history.jsonl` by hand.

If you need to know whether you run under a daemon at all: tools that need the daemon answer `DaemonMissing` or `InstanceMissing` when you do not. `DaemonMissing` means `AOS_DAEMON` is unset or its directory does not exist. `DaemonFailed` means the daemon is configured and its directory exists, but no reply arrived within the timeout (busy, paused or down). Then features like `self_tools`, `subagent`, `agents_ctl` and `thought` are unavailable for now; say so. Do not retry right away; you may try once more later.

11-06 note: The tool scratch folder is assigned by `aos-tools call`, using your stack as the parent. Brain, act and MCP callers pass their own `$AOS_STACK`; they do not append another `tools/<name>/`. Executable tools use the same stdin JSON route as folder and JSON tools. See [J3 implementation](../../thinking/2026-11/05/json-argv/10-J3到J7實作結果.md#j3-aos-tools-收口).

self_tools._description: Tool `self_tools`: add, remove or list your tools. It changes only your overlay; your definition stays as it is.

self_llm._description: Tool `self_llm`: list, change or reset your own brain settings (which model you use, temperature and so on).

self_system._description: Tool `self_system`: see, replace or reset your own system text (11-11).

self_history._description: Tool `self_history`: list, delete, summarize or replace messages in your own conversation history.

self_hook._description: Tool `self_hook`: run a program of yours when a message arrives, a tool runs, your brain fails, a tool is added, you start or stop, or a clock is due.

self_state._description: Tool `self_state`: facts and numbers about yourself (who, state, tools, llm, system, hooks, history, mailbox, children, resources, time).

self_ctl._description: Tool `self_ctl`: stop, pause, put to sleep or remove yourself.

self_tools:
# Changing your own toolbox

Tool `self_tools` is `aos-agent tools` aimed at you. It changes only your own tool list; your definition and other agents stay as they are. Changes work at once, in this turn: from your next reply you see the new list and call a new tool directly by its name (not in the same reply that added it).

One op per call (the JSON is the tool's arguments):

- list: `{"op": "ls"}`: one line per tool, its name and the first sentence of its description. `{"op": "ls", "long": true}`: one text line per tool with where it comes from, and the tools you turned off (kind `null`).
- show one in full (whole description, parameters, errors): `{"op": "get", "name": "math"}`. Use this when the one sentence from `ls` is not enough.
- add: `{"op": "add", "path": "tools/math"}`. Optional: `"name"` (default: the folder name), `"replace": true` (replace a tool with that name), `"envs": {"AOS_KNOWLEDGE": "/data/knowledge"}` (fixed values, stored as written, not for secrets), `"env_file": "secrets/read.env"` (only its location is stored; read on every call; for secrets), `"no_cache": true` (executable tools). Instead of `path`, `"path_json": {"$env": "AOS_HOME", "$path": "/lib/base/math"}` keeps the path as written and looks it up on every use.
- remove: `{"op": "rm", "name": "math"}` (a name, else a path). This turns the tool off for you; its files stay.
- undo all your changes: `{"op": "reset"}`

Rules:

- Relative paths (`path`, `env_file`, a path in `rm`/`get`) start at your workspace: `tools/math` means `$AOS_WS/tools/math`. Absolute paths are used as they are.
- Adding a tool does not create it. The folder must already exist (`PathMissing` otherwise). Write the tool files in your workspace first, or ask a human.
- `ToolExists`: a tool with that name is already there. Use `"replace": true` only if you mean to replace it.
- Unknown argument names, or an argument the op does not take, are `ArgumentsBad`.
- `DaemonMissing`: `AOS_DAEMON` is unset or its directory does not exist. `DaemonFailed`: the daemon is configured and its directory exists, but no reply arrived within the timeout (busy, paused or down). `InstanceMissing`: the daemon has no table row for you. Either way the feature is unavailable for now; say so. Do not retry right away; you may try once more later.

Why it is safe: other agents started from the same definition do not see your change. A human can see what you changed with `aos-agent ctl state --target <you>` (line `tools   own: N listed, M set to null (…)`) and undo it with `aos-agent tools reset`.
self_llm:
# Changing your own brain settings

Tool `self_llm` is `aos-agent llm` aimed at you. It changes only your own brain settings; your definition and other agents stay as they are. Changes work from your next brain call.

`model` picks your brain (a brain pack name of the llm kernel). The other keys only tune how it answers and do not change which brain you are: `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens`, `seed`, `presence_penalty`, `frequency_penalty`, `stop`. Which keys your body reads depends on what kind of agent you are (an eca agent reads only `model`).

One op per call (the JSON is the tool's arguments):

- see: `{"op": "ls"}` (one KEY=VALUE per line: the definition's settings with your changes on top); `{"op": "ls", "long": true}` also says which keys you changed (`agent`) and which come from your definition
- change: `{"op": "set", "settings": {"model": "smart-high", "temperature": "0.2"}}` (values are strings; a key your body does not read is kept anyway, with a warning line)
- undo some changes: `{"op": "rm", "keys": ["temperature"]}` (back to your definition's value; a key you did not change is `KeyMissing`)
- undo all your changes: `{"op": "reset"}`

Rules:

- Use `ls` first, and change one thing at a time.
- Nothing stops you from choosing a brain that does not work. If you do, you stop answering until a human runs `aos-agent llm --target <you> reset`. Only switch to a model you were told exists.
- A brain pack may fix some tuning keys (for example its `temperature`); then your value for that key has no effect.
- Unknown argument names, or an argument the op does not take, are `ArgumentsBad`.
- `DaemonMissing`, `DaemonFailed`, `InstanceMissing`: same as for `self_tools` (the feature is unavailable for now; say so).
self_system:
# Changing your own system text

Tool `self_system` is `aos-agent system` aimed at you; only your own copy changes, not your definition.

- see: `{"op": "get"}` (`"long": true` adds a first line FROM TAB FILE: agent, definition or none)
- change: `{"op": "set", "text": "..."}` (the whole new text; `get` first to keep the old lines)
- undo: `{"op": "reset"}`

When it works: agent-fsm = your next brain call (it replaces the definition's; empty = no system message); eca claude = your next turn (appended); eca codex = your next new conversation; an open screen = when it is reopened.

Each change makes your prompt cache miss once: change it when your job changes, not every turn. A broken text is fixed by a human: `aos-agent system --target <you> reset`. Model settings are `self_llm`. `SystemMissing` = your definition declares no system file.
self_history:
# Changing your own conversation history

Tool `self_history` is `aos-agent history` aimed at you. It lists, deletes, summarizes or replaces messages in your own conversation; other agents stay as they are. Changes work from your next turn.

Each message has a line number from 1. One op per call (the JSON is the tool's arguments):

- list: `{"op": "ls"}` (the last 20 messages, each cut at 200 characters; a first line says how many earlier ones are not shown); every message: add `"all": true`; full text: add `"long": true`; some lines only: `{"op": "ls", "range": "5-"}`; as JSON (always every message, or the range): add `"json": true`
- delete lines 3 to 4: `{"op": "rm", "range": "3-4"}`
- replace lines 1 to 6 with one message you write: `{"op": "summarize", "range": "1-6", "text": "User said their favorite color is blue."}` (the new message has role `user` unless you give `"role"`, and reads `[aos] summary: lines 1-6, 6 messages. User said their favorite color is blue.`)
- replace line 2 with a whole new message: `{"op": "set", "line": 2, "message": {"role": "user", "content": "..."}}`

A range is `"N"`, `"A-B"` or `"A-"` (A to the end).

Rules:

- Use `ls` first. Its last line tells you which lines are locked.
- The step in progress is locked: the message that called `self_history` and everything after it. Touching a locked line is `RangeBad`.
- Nothing is lost by default: removed or replaced messages move to `history_removed.jsonl` in your stack. `rm`, `summarize` and `set` accept `"keep": "FILE"` (put the originals there instead) or `"no_keep": true` (do not keep them).
- If your body is an outside CLI (eca, for example claude), a change makes your next turn start a new conversation that carries the changed record over.
- `DaemonMissing`, `DaemonFailed`, `InstanceMissing`: same as for `self_tools` (the feature is unavailable for now; say so).
self_hook:
# Hooks: run a program of yours when something happens to you

Tool `self_hook` is `aos-agent hook` aimed at you. A hook is a tool folder or an executable that runs when an event happens. It gets the event as one JSON object on stdin. Only your own hook list changes; your definition and other agents stay as they are. Changes work from the next event.

Events and their fields (every event also has `event`, `hook`, `stack`):

- `before_queue`: a message is about to enter your conversation (`letter`, `content`). Can change `content`, can drop the message.
- `after_queue`: a message entered your conversation (`letter`, `content`).
- `before_tool`: one of your tools is about to run (`name`, `id`, `arguments`). Can change `arguments`, can block the call.
- `after_tool`: a tool finished, before you see the result (`name`, `id`, `arguments`, `content`, `code`, `timed_out`). Can change `content`.
- `brain_failed`: your brain call failed (`name` = the error code, `reason`).
- `tool_added`: a new tool name appeared in your tool box (`name`, `path`).
- `after_start`: your loop started (also after a restart or a wake). `after_stop`: your loop is about to exit (`code`, `signal`; stop, sleep, removal, a failure). Not after a hard kill.
- `clock_due`: a clock moved on (`clock`, `cycle`, `interval_ms`, `last_cycle`, `missed`). Give `every_cycles` or `every_ms` (ms are counted in clock cycles, not wall time); `clock` is optional (default: `AOS_CLOCK`; or a proc name / a path). Checked at the start of each of your steps; it runs once when due, however many were missed while you were busy, and not while you sleep. The first check only notes the cycle.

One op per call:

- list: `{"op": "ls"}` (add `"long": true` to see every option and hooks you turned off)
- show one: `{"op": "get", "name": "guard"}`
- add: `{"op": "add", "event": "before_tool", "path": "hooks/guard", "condition": "peek_now_time"}`
- remove: `{"op": "rm", "name": "guard"}`
- back to your original hooks: `{"op": "reset"}`

Options of add: `name` (default: the file or folder name), `condition` (only for this tool name or error code; not for queue events), `intercept` (default true = the hook's answer counts on `before_queue`, `before_tool`, `after_tool`; false = only tell it and ignore its stdout; other events never read the answer), `async` (true = do not wait for it; its answer is then never read), `on_error` (`stop` = you stop when the hook fails, the default; `continue` = only a warning), `timeout_ms` (default 60000), `replace` (true = replace a hook with the same name).

How a hook answers (`intercept` is on by default; on the three events that can be changed):

- exit 0 and nothing on stdout: nothing changes.
- exit 0 and a JSON object on stdout (anything else on stdout is a failure; print nothing, or set `"intercept": false`): `{"content": "..."}` or `{"arguments": {...}}` replaces that field.
- exit 10: block it (the message is dropped; the tool does not run and you get the hook's stdout as the result).
- any other exit code, or a timeout: the hook failed.

A `clock_due` hook shows you nothing: your conversation gets nothing from it. To hear about it, let its program send a letter to your queue: `aos-post send STACK/queue` with `{"role": "user", "content": "..."}` (STACK = the event's `stack`). Your definition may already have a `timer` hook (every 5 minutes, does nothing): replace it with your own program under the same name.

Hooks are not checked for loops. A hook that sends you a message triggers your queue hooks again.

Errors: ArgumentsBad, OpUnknown, PathMissing, HookExists, HookMissing, HooksMissing, HooksBad, NameBad.
self_state:
# Looking at yourself: self_state

Tool `self_state` is `aos-agent ctl state` aimed at you. It only reads; it changes nothing. It is not put into your prompt by itself: call it when you want to know.

- overview, one line per part: `{}`
- some parts in detail: `{"parts": ["history", "mailbox"]}`
- every part in detail: `{"parts": ["all"]}`
- one JSON object instead of text: add `"json": true`

The ten parts: `who` (name, definition, workspace, stack), `state` (phase, letters in your queue, last answer), `tools`, `llm` (brain settings), `hooks`, `history` (how many messages, how big, the last few), `mailbox` (letters waiting), `children` (agents you started and your quota), `resources` (limits, memory and cpu time in use), `time` (now, how long you have been up).

It gives facts and numbers only, no advice. A part that cannot be read says `not available` and why; the other parts still show.

To change yourself use `self_tools`, `self_llm`, `self_history`, `self_hook`; to stop yourself use `self_ctl` (see `aos/me.json#/self_ctl`).
self_ctl:
# Stopping yourself: self_ctl

Tool `self_ctl` stops, pauses, puts to sleep or removes you, the agent calling it. To do this to another agent use `agents_ctl` (see `aos/agents.json#/agents_ctl`). Every op returns as soon as the request is sent.

- `{"op": "stop"}`: you stop at the end of this step, maybe before you answer. Your stack is kept. Someone runs `aos-agent ctl start` and you carry on from there.
- `{"op": "pause"}`: you hold still after this step. Only someone else's `aos-agent ctl resume` lets you go on.
- `{"op": "sleep"}`: you stop right away, even in the middle of this turn. `aos-agent ctl wake` or a daemon restart brings you back.
- `{"op": "rm"}`: you leave the daemon table right away; your stack is kept. Only `aos-agent ctl add` brings you back.
- `{"op": "rm", "purge": true}`: also deletes your stack (your history and everything in it). This cannot be undone.

Use it when your work is done or you must not go on. Errors: ArgumentsBad, OpUnknown, PhaseBad, CtlRejected, DaemonMissing, InstanceMissing.
